Date: 2025-05-22
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Park (Brightcart CTO), Maya Torres (Brightcart Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Brightcart Infra), Leah Cho (Brightcart PM), Luis Ortega (Redwood CS)
Recording: auto (Fireflies)
summary: Short demo of hosted generation (chat + text), focused on streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff patterns. Demo included a live Playground run, quick SDK examples, and brief discussion of security (SOC2, SSO/SAML), data handling and next-step sandbox + benchmarks. Customer is evaluating hosted for chat feature in their mobile app; main concerns: latency, cost, and data residency.
topics: Optimize suggestions: batching, KV caching, model selection
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, welcome — thanks for joining, we have about 45-55 minutes set, we'll walk through the hosted gen flow, do a short live demo in the Playground and then talk ops. Priya and I will tag-team. Um, feel free to interrupt.
[00:18] Evan Park: Hey Jordan, thanks. Quick note — we're especially interested in mobile latency and cost. We run 100k monthly MAU and want sub-350ms median for the simple Q/A path.
[00:30] Jordan Blake: Got it, that's helpful. Priya, quick context on Brightcart's typical prompt sizes?
[00:36] Priya Nair: Maya, can you share typical prompt plus expected response size?
[00:41] Maya Torres: Yeah, most are small — 40 to 120 tokens in responses, prompts average 30 tokens; but we have some longer summarization flows which go to 400-600 tokens. Also curious about streaming for UX — partial responses showing earlier.
[01:05] Jordan Blake: Great — we'll show the streaming behavior in the Playground. First, very quick architecture: hosted API -> our runtime with automatic batching and optional KV caching; routing to either the curated open model or a Redwood-verified variant. We support streaming via Server-Sent Events and websockets in our SDKs.
[01:40] Samir Patel: Do you have an idempotency pattern? If mobile retries, we want to avoid duplicate charges.
[01:48] Priya Nair: Yes — we recommend an idempotency key per user request; the backend uses that to dedup at the router layer. For long-running streams we also surface partial events with resume tokens. There was a small bug in an older SDK where resume token parsing failed on network flaps — fixed in the last patch, but the transcript generator sometimes still shows old behaviour, hehe.
[02:18] Evan Park: And how are billing tokens computed with streaming? If a client reconnects, is partial output re-billed?
[02:26] Jordan Blake: We bill by generated token count on the final output; reconnects that re-request the same generation with the same idempotency key are deduped so you won't double-bill for an identical response. If you intentionally request new generation, then it's billed. There are edge cases with partial prefix caching where we might reuse cached KV and reduce unit cost.
[02:55] Leah Cho: Can Redwood hosted do VPC peering or private networking for compliance?
[03:02] Jordan Blake: For Hosted, we don't do VPC peering; that's in Dedicated/Private. For many customers in regulated spaces, they start hosted for evaluation then move to Dedicated or Private for isolation and VPC/HSM integration. But hosted supports strong controls: SOC2, SSO (SAML/OIDC), envelope encryption via customer-managed keys in some enterprise plans. We'll send the security whitepaper.
[03:32] Maya Torres: Cool. Can we see a live stream example?
[03:36] Priya Nair: Yup — I'll share my screen and open the Playground. There may be a little lag as I switch windows.
[03:44] [screen share starts]
[04:05] Priya Nair: Ok so here's Playground -> choose Chat -> model: redwood-small-curated (demo). We'll start with temperature = 0.2, top_p = 0.95, max_tokens = 120. Note the stream checkbox is on so browser will get chunked SSEs every ~50-150ms depending on generator.
[04:28] Maya Torres: We're seeing partial tokens arriving — that's good for UX. If a chunk contains an incomplete token will you ever split mid-word?
[04:35] Priya Nair: Yes sometimes chunks split mid-token, the client reassembles; we also provide incremental text and delta operations. For mobile you usually render only when a whitespace or punctuation appears to avoid jitter.
[04:56] Evan Park: What about latency — cold vs warm model?
[05:02] Priya Nair: Cold starts are model and sequence-length dependent; for small-curated models warm RTT ~60-120ms gen latency per chunk on gpus we use for hosted. We maintain warm pools for popular models; if you see tail latency, the Console shows per-route latency histograms.
[05:30] Jordan Blake: Also Optimize will recommend quantization / model variant tradeoffs if you upload sample traffic. It can suggest smaller models or 8-bit variants that keep quality while cutting cost/latency.
[05:45] Samir Patel: How do retries look from a client perspective? Exponential backoff guidelines?
[05:50] Priya Nair: Typical pattern: client does immediate small backoff on network flaps (200-500ms), then exponential up to a few seconds; we recommend idempotency keys and include a jittered exponential (e.g., base 300ms * 2^n + jitter). For streaming we support resuming with resume token so the client doesn't need to restart from scratch.
[06:20] Evan Park: If a partial stream was delivered and it fails mid-stream, will resume token re-send earlier chunks?
[06:26] Priya Nair: Resume token points to last committed token; server will continue from there, not re-send previously committed tokens if the idempotency key + resume token match the same request.
[06:40] [crosstalk] Jordan Blake: Quick code snippet — here's Node SDK use: client.chat.create({model, messages, stream: true, idempotencyKey}). Then you attach an onData handler. We also have curl SSE example in docs.
[06:58] Maya Torres: Are there rate limits? If we spike due to release, what happens?
[07:05] Jordan Blake: Hosted has tiered rate limits by plan, and we include soft-bust policies; Optimize/Console can show token-level burn. For spikes we have burst capacity and graceful fallbacks to cheaper model variants. We can also configure per-route throttles.
[07:30] Evan Park: Could you explain KV cache briefly — what's cached and when it helps?
[07:36] Priya Nair: KV cache stores key-value attention cache for decoding. For repeated prefixes (like system prompts or conversation history that reuse prior tokens) it avoids recomputation. For short Q&A it helps less; for long-running chat sessions it can reduce latency per token. Optimize can surface hit-rate estimates given your traffic.
[07:58] Samir Patel: Anything on data retention for hosted — do you retain inputs/outputs?
[08:03] Jordan Blake: By default, hosted keeps logs for X days for debugging; enterprise plans include opt-out and stricter retention. We'll send the exact retention matrix. Also we support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest in some tiers.
[08:20] [screen — demo continued]
[08:30] Priya Nair: I'm going to intentionally force a small network drop to show resume. Ok I'm toggling network dev-tools... reconnecting... you'll see the client reconnect and request resume with the resume token.
[09:05] Maya Torres: Nice — resume took about 300ms and UI continued.
[09:12] Evan Park: What about concurrency — say 250 concurrent mobile users each with streaming sessions?
[09:20] Priya Nair: That maps to your burst and concurrency policy. For 250 concurrent streams we typically recommend a dedicated pool if sustained; for bursts hosted handles via autoscaling but SLOs may vary. We can run a spike test in the sandbox to show tail latency under concurrency.
[09:45] Leah Cho: How would we instrument cost per route?
[09:50] Jordan Blake: Console has per-route token burn, per-model median latency and cost attribution. You can break out by env, route, or token type. Also you can set cost alerts and Optimize will suggest batching settings and model swaps.
[10:15] Maya Torres: Can Optimize recommend batch sizes? Our current server syncs 8 requests then sends to the model — is that ideal?
[10:22] Priya Nair: Batching is workload-dependent. For low-latency mobile chat, smaller batch sizes with prefix caching often yield better tail latencies. Optimize will ingest sampled traffic and output suggested batch size, quantization, and an expected latency/cost delta.
[10:50] Evan Park: Any gotchas with function calling or structured outputs in streaming?
[10:56] Priya Nair: For function calling, we stream plain text until the call point, then include structured call payload. Some clients prefer waiting for full JSON to validate — streaming will send partial JSON which you may want to buffer until valid parse. Parser resilience on client side is important.
[11:18] Samir Patel: Ok, security — SSO and audit logs?
[11:23] Jordan Blake: Hosted supports SAML SSO and RBAC; audit logs are available as an add-on with retention windows. For stricter compliance we suggest Dedicated/Private which include network isolation and HSM integration.
[11:40] Evan Park: Could you share pricing ballpark? We're looking for cost per 1M tokens generated with small model.
[11:48] Jordan Blake: We'll send a tailored pricing sheet after we see sample traffic; ballpark for small curated model is $X per 1M tokens — we'll include a detailed estimate in the follow-up.
[12:05] Leah Cho: Next steps?
[12:08] Jordan Blake: Proposed: 1) we send sandbox invite + security docs (SOC2, retention). 2) Brightcart shares representative prompts/logs (anonymized) for Optimize run. 3) Redwood runs a short concurrency spike test in the sandbox and shares results. Does that work?
[12:24] Maya Torres: Yes. Also please include the resume token notes and idempotency examples in the quickstart.
[12:31] Jordan Blake: Will do. Luis — any handoff notes?
[12:35] Luis Ortega: I'll include a checklist in the invite: onboarding steps, contacts, and a POC template.
[12:42] Evan Park: Great. Thanks all.
[12:45] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and sandbox invite.
[12:50] [meeting end — short outro and recording stops]
